summary: The EX90 is Volvo's electric flagship and, alongside the six-seat Cadillac Vistiq, the only luxury-badged three-row battery SUV on sale in Australia. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the cabin, the quietness and the safety case -- ANCAP tested it in 2025 and it returned the highest adult occupant protection score of any vehicle rated that year -- while splitting over the ride, which is terse on the passive Plus and floaty-then-bouncy on the Ultra's air springs. The MY26 rebuild onto an 800-volt architecture with a 106kWh pack and 350kW DC charging fixed the launch car's biggest weakness, but at $124,990 and $134,990 before on-road costs the range clears the $91,661 FBT threshold by a wide margin and Volvo is about to reopen it $18,000 lower with a single-motor base grade.
pros: ANCAP rated the EX90 five stars on 2025 test protocols with 92 per cent adult occupant protection -- the highest score of any vehicle ANCAP rated in 2025 -- plus 94 per cent child occupant protection, 82 per cent vulnerable road user and 84 per cent safety assist

Ownership costs are close to nil beyond tyres and electricity for five years: a 5-year/unlimited-kilometre unconditional warranty, 8 years of drive-battery cover, 5 years roadside assistance, and scheduled servicing to 5 years/150,000km included in the purchase price at $0

The MY26 switch from 400 to 800 volts lifted DC fast-charging from 250kW to a 350kW peak, and Volvo Australia quotes 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes -- a Cadillac Vistiq, its only luxury three-row electric rival here, peaks at 130kW

Rated to tow 2,200kg braked and genuinely seats seven adults on individual sliding second-row seats, in a segment where the Audi and BMW alternatives at this money are five-seaters and a Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV starts at $197,200 before on-road costs

Volvo quotes a 0.29 drag coefficient and Australian testers single out the cabin as one of the quietest they have measured, with CarExpert rating its Pilot Assist and lane-keeping calibration ahead of the Polestar and Zeekr cars that share the same Geely software stack
cons: Neither grade comes near the electric-car FBT exemption: the cheapest EX90 is $124,990 before on-road costs, roughly $33,000 above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold, and about $10,000 of that sticker is luxury car tax

Volvo replaces the entry Plus Twin Motor with a $106,990 Plus Single Motor in September/October 2026, an $18,000 cut to the range's opening price within months, on top of a MY26 change from 400V to 800V that leaves every launch car on the slower architecture -- both point to weak early resale
Australia gets the EX90 as a seven-seater only, with no six-seat captain's-chair layout of the kind offered on the Kia EV9 GT and Cadillac Vistiq, and only 324 litres behind the third row

Reviewers agree the primary ride never settles: CarExpert found the passively sprung Plus on 20-inch wheels 'a little busy and jittery' over pockmarked roads, and CarsGuide found the Ultra's twin-chamber air suspension 'bouncy over bigger bumps, especially over the rear axle'

At 2,764kg and a claimed 22.8kWh/100km it is thirstier than a Hyundai Ioniq 9 or Kia EV9 on the same duty cycle, and its 521km WLTP range is well short of the 570km the pre-update launch cars advertised
